meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Epictetus (Discourses III.23.1). The precise English phrasing is Elizabeth Carter's 1758 translation — the first complete English Epictetus.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: c. 50 – c. 135 AD · Greek Stoic philosopher, born enslaved
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Epictetus, from his Discourses (III.23.1), as recorded by his pupil Arrian. The exact English wording you see is Elizabeth Carter’s 1758 translation — her line reads “First say to yourself, what you would be; and then do, what you have to do,” and the popular version simply drops two of her commas.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Elizabeth Carter, All the Works of Epictetus (London, 1758)
Greek: “Τίς εἶναι θέλεις; σαυτῷ πρῶτον εἰπέ· εἶθ’ οὕτως ποίει ἃ ποιεῖς.”

source.excerpt: First say to yourself, what you would be; and then do, what you have to do. For, in almost everything, we see this to be the practice. Those who follow athletic exercises, first determine what they would be, and then act accordingly.
trail: Wikiquote places the line in the main Discourses section at III.23.1, with the Schenkl Greek text ↗ — not in any “Misattributed” list.
The exact popular wording tracks Elizabeth Carter’s 1758 rendering ↗: “First say to yourself, what you would be; and then do, what you have to do.”
Other translators phrase it quite differently — George Long’s 1877 version reads “First say to yourself Who you wish to be: then do accordingly what you are doing” ↗.
Carter’s Epictetus was first published in 1758 — the first complete English translation ↗ of the Stoic’s works.
source.excerptNote: Carter’s 1758 wording opens Discourses III.23; Epictetus goes on to illustrate the maxim with athletes, who first decide what they want to be and then train for it.

sourceLink.text: Carter’s translation of Discourses III.23 on Wikisource

source.rightsNote: The wording shown is Elizabeth Carter’s translation, first published in London in 1758 — well before 1931, so it is public domain in the United States, as is the ancient Greek original. Note that a modern translation of the same passage (e.g. Oldfather’s Loeb or a later Penguin/Oxford edition) would carry its own separate copyright.

author.metaLine: c. 50 – c. 135 AD · Greek Stoic philosopher (Nicopolis)
author.bio: Epictetus was a Greek Stoic philosopher born into slavery at Hierapolis in Phrygia. After gaining his freedom he taught in Rome and later founded a school at Nicopolis in Epirus. He wrote nothing himself; his teaching survives only because his pupil Arrian transcribed it as the Discourses and the Enchiridion.

misattribution.heading: The wording is a translator's, not a raw quote
misattribution.intro: The thought is authentically Epictetus, but the polished one-liner people share is a specific 18th-century English translation — usually passed off as if Epictetus said these exact words.

items.why: Epictetus taught in Greek and wrote nothing down. This precise English wording is Elizabeth Carter’s 1758 rendering ↗; other translators phrase it quite differently, so “Epictetus said” really means “Carter translated.”
Carter’s line has two commas — “First say to yourself, what you would be; and then do, what you have to do” — which the popular version drops, a small modernization rarely noted.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Epictetus (Discourses III.23.1 ↗) — but the exact words are Elizabeth Carter’s 1758 translation, lightly repunctuated.

context.heading: Decide who you are, then act
lead: The maxim opens a chapter of the Discourses in which Epictetus warns against philosophizing for applause. His point is order of operations: settle your character first, then let your conduct follow from it.
He drives it home with the athlete: a competitor first decides what he wants to be, and only then submits to the diet, the training, and the discipline that identity demands.
